extracted.intended_audience: applicants, patent attorneys/agents, and practitioners filing PCT (international) applications with the USPTO (U.S. Receiving Office) or interacting with US PCT Authorities
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive rules and criteria for preparing, filing, correcting, and prosecuting PCT international applications through the U.S. Receiving Office (and interactions with the IB, ISA, and IPEA), including fees, priority claims, correspondence, transmissions, and remedies for errors or delays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refunds of International, Search, Supplemental Search, Handling, and Transmittal Fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Conditions under which various PCT-related fees are refundable to applicants (international fee, search fee, supplemental search fee, handling fee, transmittal fee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: International and search fees refunded if no international filing date is accorded or if the application is withdrawn before transmittal of the record copy to the International Bureau (PCT Rules 15.6 and 16.2). The search fee will be refunded if the application is withdrawn before transmittal of the search copy to the International Searching Authority. The transmittal fee will not be refunded. The handling fee (§ 1.482(b)) will be refunded (PCT Rule 57.6) only if (1) the Demand is withdrawn before the Demand has been sent by the IPEA to the IB, or (2) the Demand is considered not to have been submitted (PCT Rule 54.4(a)). Refund of the supplemental search fee will be made if determined warranted by the Director or designee under PCT Rule 40.2(c), and specifically will be made if the applicant is successful in a protest filed pursuant to 37 CFR 1.477 to a holding of lack of unity of invention (the supplemental search fee must be paid and accompanied by a protest and a request for refund). If the Receiving Office and ISA are not the same, any request for refund of the search fee made after transmittal of the search copy must be directed to the ISA, not the Receiving Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority Claim: Required Contents and Timing for Claiming or Correcting Priority
rubrics_metrics.description: What an applicant must indicate to claim priority of one or more earlier national, regional or international applications and the time limits for correcting or adding priority claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant must indicate on the Request at time of filing the country, filing date, and application number of the earlier application (see PCT Article 8 and PCT Rule 4.10). Under PCT Rule 26bis.1 and 37 CFR 1.451 and 1.465, an applicant may correct or add a priority claim by notice to the Receiving Office or the IB within 16 months from the priority date (or, if the priority date is changed, within 16 months of the changed date), whichever expires first, and in any event until 4 months from the international filing date. The certified copy of the earlier application may be filed with the international application or submitted to the IB or Receiving Office not later than 16 months from the priority date (special provisions if early processing requested). RO/US may prepare and electronically transmit a certified copy if requested (Form PCT/RO/101 and PCT Rule 17.1(b)); IB may obtain copies from digital libraries under PCT Rule 17.1(b‑bis). Transmission of the priority document may be delayed or prevented where no inventor is common to the priority application and the international application, or until national security review is complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restoration of the Right of Priority (37 CFR 1.452 / PCT Rule 26bis.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: When and how an applicant may request restoration of the right of priority if the international application was filed after the priority period but within two months of its expiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restoration is available if the international filing date is later than the priority period expiration but within two months and the delay was unintentional (USPTO applies the 'unintentional' standard). A request must be filed not later than two months from the expiration of the priority period and must include: (1) a notice under PCT Rule 26bis.1(a) adding the priority claim if missing, (2) the petition fee (§ 1.17(m)), and (3) a statement that the delay was unintentional. The Director may require additional information. If the applicant requested early publication and the required items are filed after the IB has completed technical preparations for publication, those items are considered not submitted in time. Note: PCT Rule 26bis.3 also contemplates an 'in spite of due care' standard (IB decides under both standards); applicants desiring 'in spite of due care' restoration may file directly with IB as receiving Office because RO/US only decides under 'unintentional'. Restored priority may not be recognized by some national Offices that have notified incompatibility—see WIPO list; restored PCT priority is effective in the U.S. national stage if restored during the international stage. Regardless, the priority date governs PCT time limits (PCT Article 2(xi)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-transmission (withholding) of Documents Related to Restoration Requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria under which the Receiving Office may withhold transmission of documents or parts thereof in relation to a request for restoration of priority under PCT Rule 26bis.3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Receiving Office shall, upon reasoned request by the applicant or sua sponte, not transmit documents or parts thereof if it finds that: (i) the document or part does not obviously serve the purpose of informing the public about the international application; (ii) publication or public access would clearly prejudice the personal or economic interests of any person; and (iii) there is no prevailing public interest to grant access (PCT Rule 26bis.3(h‑bis)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to Continuation or Continuation‑in‑Part / Parent Application Indication (PCT Rule 4.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: How to indicate in the Request that an international application should be treated as a continuation or continuation‑in‑part of an earlier application and how to identify the parent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the applicant intends the international application to be treated in any designated State as a continuation or continuation‑in‑part, the Request shall so indicate and identify the relevant parent application or parent patent/grant. Use the Supplemental Box of the Request to identify an earlier pending U.S. nonprovisional or international application designating the U.S., specifying the parent application number, the relationship ('continuation' or 'continuation‑in‑part'), and the filing date if the parent is an international application. Corrections/additions to such indications may be made by notice to the IB within 16 months from the priority date (PCT Rule 26quater.1); late notices received after technical preparations for publication are treated as received on the last day of the time limit if received before publication prep completes. Inclusion of a proper reference in the PCT Request or on the front page of the published international application satisfies 37 CFR 1.78 benefit-claim requirements for national stage; omission may waive the right to rely on the prior application in later filings (see MPEP § 211.02).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of PCT Transmittal Forms (Form PTO‑1382) to Simplify Filings
rubrics_metrics.description: Availability and intended use of a PCT international application transmittal letter/form to simplify filing with the U.S. Receiving Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form PTO‑1382 is available for applicants when filing PCT international applications and related documents with the U.S. Receiving Office to simplify filing; the form can be obtained online at the USPTO PCT forms webpage. (Advisory: use of the form is recommended to simplify filing but is not a substantive substitute for complying with PCT/US requirements.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign Filing License Requirements and Practice (35 U.S.C. 368; 37 CFR 5.x)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a license for foreign filing is required to forward/transmit an international application to foreign patent offices or authorities and practical consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A foreign filing license is not required to file an international application in the U.S. Receiving Office but may be required before the applicant or RO/US can forward a copy to a foreign patent office, the IB, or other foreign authority (35 U.S.C. 368, 37 CFR 5.1 and 5.11). A license is not required if (1) the invention was not made in the United States; or (2) a U.S. national application was filed at least six months earlier, is not subject to a secrecy order, and the international application does not change the general nature of the invention (37 CFR 5.11, 5.15). In other cases, applicant should petition for a license for foreign filing (37 CFR 5.12) and identify any additional subject matter (37 CFR 5.14(c)). If no petition is included and it is clear a license is required, current practice is to construe the filing as including a request for a license; if grantable, it will be issued without further correspondence; if not, applicant will be contacted. A foreign filing license also authorizes export of technical data abroad for preparing/filing/prosecuting a foreign application; special caution about exporting technical data into WIPO ePCT without separately complying with U.S. export control and DOE regulations (22 CFR, 15 CFR, 10 CFR) — see MPEP §§ 140 and 1821.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of a Secrecy Order on International Applications
rubrics_metrics.description: How the application of a secrecy order affects transmittal to IB and potential abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a secrecy order is applied to an international application, the application will not be forwarded to the IB while the secrecy order remains in effect (PCT Article 27(8) and 35 U.S.C. 368). If the secrecy order remains in effect so the Record Copy is not received in time by the IB, the international application will be declared withdrawn (abandoned) (37 CFR 5.3(d), PCT Article 12(3), PCT Rule 22.3). It may be possible to prevent abandonment as to the United States (if designated) by fulfilling 35 U.S.C. 371(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence Requirements: Need for Letter, Signature, and Identification (PCT Rule 92.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements that papers (other than the international application itself) be accompanied by a signed letter identifying the international application, and consequences for non-compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any paper submitted in the international procedure (other than the international application itself), if not itself in the form of a letter, must be accompanied by a letter identifying the international application and shall be signed by the applicant (PCT Rule 92.1). If not complied with, the applicant is informed of the non‑compliance and invited to remedy it within a reasonable time fixed in the invitation (not less than 10 days and not more than 1 month from mailing). If remedied within the time limit, the omission is disregarded; otherwise the paper is disregarded. If non‑compliance was overlooked and the paper taken into account, the non‑compliance shall be disregarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Languages for Correspondence (PCT Rule 92.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Permitted languages for letters/documents to ISA, IPEA, and the International Bureau and exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any letter or document submitted by the applicant to the ISA or IPEA shall be in the same language as the international application unless a translation has been transmitted or the Authority authorizes another language (PCT Rules 55.1, 55.3, 23.1). Any letter from the applicant to the International Bureau must be in English or French; any letter or notification from the IB to applicant or any national Office shall be in English or French. ISA/IPEA may authorize use of other languages for letters to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of an International Application with Two or More Applicants
rubrics_metrics.description: How to identify an international application for correspondence purposes when multiple applicants are listed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an international application indicates two or more applicants, it is sufficient for identification purposes to indicate the name of the applicant first named in the request in any Form or correspondence relating to that application. (The first-sentence rule does not apply to the Demand.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing by Mail: Priority Mail Express Date Acceptance and Limitations of Certificate of Mailing
rubrics_metrics.description: How certain mailing procedures affect the effective filing date and limits on use of the certificate of mailing to secure a filing date during the international stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPS Priority Mail Express® procedure (37 CFR 1.10) applies to papers filed with the USPTO in international applications; papers will be accorded the 'date accepted' on the Priority Mail Express® label if the provisions of 37 CFR 1.10 are complied with (include mailing label number on each paper or fee; if multiple papers, use cover letter itemizing papers and include label number). The certificate of mailing under 37 CFR 1.8 cannot be used to obtain a date of deposit for submissions during the international stage if the date of deposit is desired: submissions using 1.8 will be accorded the date of receipt unless the receipt date falls on a non-working day (37 CFR 1.6(a)(1)). Thus, certificate of mailing procedures of 37 CFR 1.8 are not available to have a submission considered timely filed if not physically received on or before the due date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing by Facsimile: Permitted Submissions, Exceptions, and Receipt/Signature Rules (PCT Rule 92.4; 37 CFR 1.6(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Which documents may (and may not) be filed by fax with the USPTO during the international stage, how receipt dates are determined, and rules about signatures on faxed documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PCT Rule 92.4 allows national Offices to receive documents by facsimile; USPTO accepts facsimile transmissions with certain exceptions identified in 37 CFR 1.6(d). A facsimile is not permitted (and will not be accorded a date of receipt) if the document is: (A) required by statute to be certified; (B) a color drawing under 37 CFR 1.437; (C) an international application for patent; or (D) a copy of the international application and the basic national fee for entering the national stage (37 CFR 1.6(d)). Facsimile may be used for substitute sheets (other than color drawings), extensions of time, power of attorney, fee authorizations (other than the basic national fee), demands, responses to written opinions, oaths/declarations, petitions, Article 34 amendments, and translations. A Certificate of Transmission under 37 CFR 1.8(a)(1) may be used except in instances excluded by 1.8(a)(2); note the Certificate of Transmission cannot be used for filing an international application or correspondence in an international application before USPTO, the U.S. ISA, or U.S. IPEA. A signature on a document received via facsimile in a permitted situation is acceptable (PCT Rule 92.4(b); 37 CFR 1.4(d)(1)(ii)). The receipt date of a faxed document is the date the USPTO completes the transmission unless that date is a Saturday, Sunday, or Federal holiday, in which case the next succeeding non-holiday is the date of receipt (37 CFR 1.6(a)(3)). Documents illegible or partially received are treated as not received to the extent illegible or not received (PCT Rule 92.4(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Irregularities in Mail or Electronic Communications Service (PCT Rule 82 and 82quater)
rubrics_metrics.description: When delays or losses in mail or interruptions of electronic communications excuse failure to meet PCT time limits and what evidence is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay or loss in the mail may be excused if the party proves to the satisfaction of the Receiving Office that the document was mailed at least five days before the expiration of the time limit and mailed by registered airmail (or registered surface mail where surface mail normally arrives within two days) (PCT Rule 82.1(a)–(c)). If mailing is proven, delay is excused or substitution of a new copy is permitted, but evidence and, where applicable, substitute document must be submitted within one month after the party noticed or should have noticed the delay, and in no case later than six months after the expiration of the time limit. Similar provisions apply where a delivery service other than postal authorities is used if the national Office notifies the IB. Interruption in mail or electronic communications service (war, strike, natural calamity, epidemic, general unavailability of electronic communications) can excuse delays or extend time limits where the outage affected a widespread area, was unexpected or unforeseen, and no alternative means were available (see PCT Rule 82quater and Administrative Instruction Section 111). PCT Rule 80.5 addresses periods expiring on non‑working days.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rectification of Obvious Mistakes (PCT Rule 91)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an obvious mistake in the international application or other documents may be rectified and which authority is competent to authorize rectification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An obvious mistake in the international application or another document may be rectified if the applicant requests it (PCT Rule 91.1). Authorization is by the 'competent authority': receiving Office for mistakes in the request; International Searching Authority for mistakes in the description, claims or drawings (unless IPEA is competent as in (iii)); IPEA if a demand for international preliminary examination has been made and the date for examination has passed; and the Office/Authority/Bureau for other documents not referred to in (i)-(iii) (except abstract or Article 19 amendments). The competent authority shall authorize rectification only if it is obvious to that authority that, as at the applicable date, something else was intended than what appears and that nothing else could have been intended than the proposed rectification. For mistakes in description/claims/drawings, the competent authority may only take into account the contents of the description, claims and drawings (and any relevant correction/amendment) when deciding obviousness under paragraph (c).
